officialDocs.label: Set up a global OAuth client
Submit your app to the Marketplace

verdict.summary: OAuth clients are per Zendesk subdomain, so a local client only works for one account; to let any Zendesk customer connect you need Zendesk to convert your client into a global OAuth client, which requires a d3v- sponsored partner account, and since August 2025 multi-customer integrations must also be submitted for Marketplace review. Using a customer's API token or their own OAuth client is now banned by the Developer Terms, so there is no self-serve shortcut for a commercial agent.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Start a free 14-day trial, create a local OAuth client in Admin Center, and run the authorization code flow against that subdomain. No review is needed for a local client.

timeToProd.assumes: A server-side agent that reads and writes tickets across many customers' Zendesk accounts, which needs a global OAuth client plus a Marketplace listing; there is no faster path for third parties.
timeToProd.waitingOn: Sponsored d3v- account approval (no stated SLA), the global OAuth client request (no stated SLA), and Marketplace review (1–3 weeks for new apps).

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Only the Marketplace review window (1–3 weeks) is stated by Zendesk. Sponsored-account and global-client approval times are not published, so the total is an estimate.

verdict.cost: Free: trial and sponsored developer accounts cost nothing. Customers' API rate limits depend on their Zendesk plan.

prerequisites.item: A Zendesk Support trial with a subdomain starting d3v-, converted to a sponsored account
prerequisites.why: Global OAuth requests are only accepted from d3v- subdomains, and sponsored accounts are reserved for developers building for the Marketplace.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Sponsored accounts don't expire after the 14-day trial and cover up to 5 agents.

prerequisites.item: An organization registered on the Zendesk Marketplace developer portal
prerequisites.why: Both the global OAuth request form and Marketplace submissions live in that portal.

prerequisites.item: An HTTPS redirect URL and a confidential server to hold the client secret
prerequisites.why: Confidential clients authenticate with a secret (or PKCE) when exchanging the code; public clients must use PKCE.

prerequisites.item: Refresh token handling in your token store
prerequisites.why: New global clients get 30-minute access tokens by default, and Zendesk says refresh support is required for global clients from January 31, 2026.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The refresh-token page itself says the adoption deadline is April 1, 2027 and its FAQ says adoption is optional, so the sources conflict on the hard deadline.

scopeTiers.tier: Single-account (local client, your own or one customer's instance)
scopeTiers.impact: Any scope works for a local client, but only on the subdomain where it was created. Fine for development and for a customer building their own internal integration. Third parties may not use a customer's own OAuth client to serve that customer.

scopeTiers.tier: Read-only resource scopes on a global client
scopeTiers.impact: Enough for an agent that summarizes or searches tickets. Zendesk's Marketplace Operations team sets 'allowed scopes' on your global client, and anything outside that list fails with invalid_scope.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Zendesk doesn't say whether narrower scopes speed up approval. Grouping them separately is our reading of the allowed-scopes mechanism.

scopeTiers.tier: Write scopes on a global client
scopeTiers.impact: Needed for agents that reply to, tag, or update tickets. Same global-client and Marketplace path; justify write access in the request.
Lets an admin's token make requests on behalf of end users. Expect extra scrutiny; it has to be in your client's allowed scopes.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: No source says how often impersonate is granted to global clients.

steps.title: Start a Zendesk trial with a d3v- subdomain
steps.detail: Sign up for a free Zendesk Support trial and choose a subdomain that starts with d3v- (for example d3v-yourcompany).

steps.title: Request sponsorship for the account
steps.detail: Fill in the Sponsored Account Request Form linked from the sponsored-account page so the trial doesn't expire.

steps.title: Wait for sponsored-account approval
steps.detail: Zendesk emails you when the trial becomes a sponsored account. Build against the trial meanwhile.

steps.title: Create a local OAuth client prepared for global conversion
steps.detail: In Admin Center > Apps and integrations > APIs > OAuth clients, add a client of kind Confidential. Prefix the Unique Identifier with zdg-, fill every field (including 'optional' ones), use production names and redirect URLs, and copy the secret, which is shown once.

steps.title: Implement the authorization code flow
steps.detail: Send users to https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/oauth/authorizations/new with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope and state (plus code_challenge/S256 if using PKCE). Ask the user for their subdomain first. Exchange the code within 120 seconds at POST https://{subdomain}.zendesk.com/oauth/tokens. Store tokens per subdomain.

steps.title: Add refresh-token handling
steps.detail: Request tokens with expires_in/refresh_token_expires_in within the allowed ranges, refresh via grant_type=refresh_token, and atomically save the new refresh token because the old pair is invalidated.

steps.title: Register your organization on the Marketplace portal
steps.detail: Sign in to the Marketplace developer portal and create your organization profile.

steps.title: Draft the global OAuth request
steps.detail: List only the scopes you need with a short justification each, and confirm the d3v- subdomain and zdg- identifier match the local client.

steps.title: Submit the global OAuth request
steps.detail: In the Marketplace portal choose Global OAuth > Request new OAuth and submit. Add support@appsubmission.zendesk.com to your contacts so updates aren't filtered.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Older docs call the tab Organization > Global OAuth Request.

steps.title: Wait for global client approval
steps.detail: Zendesk replies with a ticket reference. On approval the local client is converted to global and you lose access to its admin page.

steps.title: Prepare and submit the Marketplace listing
steps.detail: Build the ZIP for an integration (marketingOnly: true) app with marketing assets and translations, and draft the listing copy. After acceptance, send the app ID and organization ID headers on every Zendesk API call. A human uploads and submits.

steps.title: Marketplace review
steps.detail: Zendesk reviews new submissions in about 1–3 weeks (1–2 weeks for updates).

agentCanDo: Implement the subdomain-aware OAuth flow with state and PKCE
Build refresh-token rotation and invalid_grant recovery
Draft the global OAuth scope list and justifications
Build the Marketplace ZIP, manifest and listing copy
Add the integration identification headers to API calls
Handle per-plan rate limits and 429 Retry-After
humanMustDo: Create the d3v- trial and file the sponsored-account form
Create the zdg- OAuth client in Admin Center and save the secret
Register the Marketplace organization and submit the global OAuth request
Upload and submit the Marketplace app
Customer side: a Zendesk user authorizes access on their subdomain

blockers.symptom: Customers on other subdomains get an error or can't find your client when authorizing
blockers.cause: Local OAuth clients only work on the subdomain where they were created.
blockers.fix: Request a global OAuth client from a d3v- sponsored account.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The exact error string wasn't documented in the pages we read.

blockers.cause: Submitted from a subdomain without the d3v- prefix, or the local client identifier lacks the zdg- prefix.
blockers.fix: Create the client in a d3v- sponsored account with a zdg- identifier and resubmit.

blockers.cause: Your app asked for a scope outside the global client's allowed scopes set by Zendesk.
blockers.fix: Request only allowed scopes, or contact Zendesk Support mentioning 'global oauth allowed scopes' and your client_id to change them.

blockers.cause: A stale refresh token was reused; each refresh invalidates the previous access and refresh token.
blockers.fix: Persist the new refresh token atomically and serialize refreshes per connection.

blockers.symptom: Token exchange fails even though the user just approved
blockers.cause: The authorization code is only valid for 120 seconds.
blockers.fix: Exchange the code immediately in the callback handler.

blockers.symptom: Lost the client secret after global approval
blockers.cause: Converting to a global client removes your access to the client administration page.
blockers.fix: Save identifier and secret before submitting; otherwise contact Zendesk Support.

nuances.text: Since August 2025, Zendesk's Developer Terms bar third parties from authenticating with a customer's API token or the customer's own OAuth client, and multi-customer apps must go through Marketplace review. Private apps customers build for their own use are exempt.

Token lifetimes: new global clients (from February 2, 2026) and new local clients (from April 30, 2026) default to 30-minute access tokens and 30-day refresh tokens. Access tokens can be set from 5 minutes to 48 hours and refresh tokens from 7 to 90 days.

Rate limits are per customer plan: 200 requests/min on Team, 400 on Growth/Professional, 700 on Enterprise, 2,500 with High Volume API or Enterprise Plus. Your agent's throughput depends on each customer's plan.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The page doesn't say whether the limit is shared with the customer's other integrations; we assume it is.

nuances.text: OAuth is per subdomain: the authorize and token URLs include the customer's subdomain, so your connect UI has to ask for it, and host-mapped domains can't be used for OAuth.
Scopes can be broad (read, write) or resource-specific (tickets:read, users:write). Leaving scopes empty on a client allows all of them.
If the admin who created a client loses permission to manage OAuth clients, client-credentials tokens stop working but authorization-code tokens keep working.
Global clients can't be used to build Sunshine Conversations bots, and Zendesk Sell uses a separate Multi-User Application instead of global OAuth.
